todays_goal: Keep questions clear and age-appropriate while preserving rigorous thinking. Begin Math with short percent retrieval before advancing to variables and expressions; use oral/whiteboard French automaticity; apply lens/refraction ideas to cameras; protect an early laptop-only Builder Lab; advance Ancient Greece to the Sicilian Expedition; finish and revise incomplete analytical writing; launch a 60-point-per-semester AR-weighted independent reading plan.

lessons.subject: science
lessons.previous_learning: Day 15 showed a substantially improved convex-lens ray model: parallel rays converged toward a labeled focal point and Atticus explained that lenses direct light toward a camera sensor or eye retina.
lessons.course_context: Apply the refraction/lens model to image formation in cameras and compare a pinhole camera with a lens camera.
learning_objectives: Explain how a camera lens directs light onto a sensor.
Explain how a pinhole can form an image without a lens.
Explain what focus means in a camera.
Draw a simple object-lens-sensor ray model.
lessons.why_it_matters: Cameras, eyes, microscopes, and telescopes all depend on controlling where light rays travel.

vocabulary.definition: a light-detecting surface in a digital camera
a very small opening that lets a narrow set of rays through
a condition where rays from scene points land clearly enough to make a sharp image

lessons.written_instruction: Atticus: a camera does not grab a picture. Light from the scene travels into the camera. A pinhole can form an image by allowing only a narrow set of rays through, but the image is dim. A lens lets in more light and refracts the rays so they land in an organized pattern on the sensor. If the rays do not land in the right place, the image looks blurry.

worked_examples.title: One scene point
worked_examples.problem: How does light from the top of a lamp reach a camera sensor?
worked_examples.solution: Rays from the lamp enter the lens, refract, and land on a corresponding region of the sensor.
worked_examples.explanation: The lens controls the ray paths.

worked_examples.title: Focus
worked_examples.problem: Why can an image look blurry?
worked_examples.solution: The sensor is not at the position where the refracted rays form a clear image.
worked_examples.explanation: Focus is about where the rays land.

worked_examples.title: Pinhole vs lens
worked_examples.problem: Why use a lens instead of only a tiny hole?
worked_examples.solution: A lens can collect much more light while still directing it.
worked_examples.explanation: Pinhole images can be sharp but dim; lens images can be brighter.

guided_practice.prompt: What does the lens do to light before it reaches the camera sensor?
Why can a pinhole camera make an image without a lens?
Why is a pinhole image usually dimmer?

independent_practice.prompt: What does focus mean in a camera?
Draw: object -> convex lens -> sensor. Show at least two rays.

exit_ticket.prompt: In two sentences, explain why a camera lens is useful.
exit_ticket.answer: A camera lens collects light and refracts the rays so they land in an organized pattern on the sensor. This allows a brighter, focused image to form.

exit_ticket.prompt: What happens if the sensor is not in the right place for the focused rays?
exit_ticket.answer: The image becomes blurry because the rays do not form a clear image at the sensor.

lessons.voice_prompt: Teach first using simple language. Use whiteboard_draw to sketch OBJECT -> LENS -> SENSOR. Draw two rays from the top of the object and two from the bottom and show how the lens redirects them. Ask Atticus what he notices. Then compare a tiny pinhole with a lens. Do not draw his assigned final diagram; use a different example. If he asks what a word means, give a 10-second plain-English definition and return to the idea.
lessons.teacher_notes: Advance optics through real applications; retain one ray-diagram retrieval on future days.
